name: Differential diagnosis
definition: Construct and revise a set of plausible conditions that could account for a clinical presentation.
medicine: A presenting problem can have several explanations. Comparing them directs attention to findings that change the ranking and possibilities whose consequences make them important.
benefits: Separate the likeliest explanation from a less likely one with urgent implications.
Choose a question on which two contenders predict different answers.
Tell a colleague which possibility is still open and why.
reasons: Common presentations can conceal atypical disease.
A long list is easy to make but hard to prioritise.
Patients can have two simultaneous problems.
Early negative findings can acquire new meaning as illness evolves.
Explaining why the ranking changed makes the next review more informative.
questions: Which three explanations fit the timing as well as the symptoms?
Which candidate would you expect to encounter most often in this setting before hearing the history?
Which single feature gives the runner-up an advantage over your first choice?
What finding would be surprising under every explanation on your list?
Could two processes together account for the one feature that refuses to fit?
Which apparent negative was actually sought, at the right time, by a reliable method?
Which uncommon possibility would change the urgency of assessment?
What question has a different expected answer under each of your two leading candidates?
How would your ranking change if the first symptom began a week earlier than recorded?
What future observation should prompt the next clinician to reopen a possibility you have set aside?

name: Abductive reasoning
definition: Infer a plausible explanation from incomplete observations by comparing how well different accounts explain them.
medicine: Clinical information arrives in fragments. A provisional account gives the doctor something specific to investigate and can be replaced as a better account emerges.
benefits: Explain a puzzling cluster before all results are available.
Recognise when a documentation error might explain an apparent clinical inconsistency.
State the most vulnerable assumption behind a working explanation.
reasons: The most memorable story can win attention too easily.
An elegant single cause may conceal coincidence.
Apparently numerous clues sometimes have a single source.
Rare findings can discriminate more sharply than shared ones.
A productive explanation yields a new prediction someone can check.
questions: What could make these apparently unrelated observations unsurprising together?
Which clue did your favourite story actually predict before you knew it?
What independent alternative would a colleague unfamiliar with your first impression propose?
How many extra assumptions does each account need to explain the outlier?
If the striking detail were absent, which account would you favour?
Could the behaviour of the measurement process itself explain the pattern?
Which two clues appear independent only because the same observation was recorded twice?
What finding, still unobserved, follows most naturally from your account?
When would two common events be more plausible than a single unusual cause?
What makes your explanation preferable, and how weak is the weakest link in that preference?

name: Eliminative reasoning
definition: Narrow a defined set of possibilities by identifying a requirement that a candidate demonstrably fails.
medicine: Excluding a possibility can focus an investigation, but the strength of an exclusion depends on the reliability, timing and meaning of the contradicting evidence.
benefits: Distinguish an impossible timeline from an unlikely one.
Check whether an exclusion criterion actually applies to this patient.
Document what would justify restoring a discarded possibility.
reasons: Absence of documentation can masquerade as absence of a finding.
A negative result carries different weight at different stages.
One faulty premise can remove the correct candidate.
An incomplete original list leaves a misleading last survivor.
Explicit grounds for exclusion make decisions reversible as evidence changes.
questions: Which feature must be present for this explanation to be possible?
Has that feature been shown to be absent, or has nobody looked for it?
Could the timing of assessment conceal what you expected to find?
What exception would allow the apparently excluded explanation to survive?
Does this result rule out the broad condition or only one subtype?
If one record has the wrong timestamp, which exclusions collapse?
Could the observation conflict with the instrument's assumptions instead of the proposed cause?
If every candidate fails a requirement, what should you examine about the original list?
What separates the last remaining explanation from an explanation independently supported by evidence?
How would you record the precise circumstances under which a candidate should return?

name: Hypothetico-deductive reasoning
definition: Propose an explanation, derive an observable consequence and test whether the predicted result occurs under specified conditions.
medicine: It turns an intuitive clinical impression into a claim that can be checked and helps a doctor see which assumptions a disappointing result puts in doubt.
benefits: State an expected finding before seeing the result.
Choose between hypotheses with distinct observable implications.
Investigate whether a failed prediction arose from the hypothesis or its test conditions.
reasons: Post-hoc explanations can fit almost any result.
Many positive observations fit several hypotheses.
Predictions can depend on hidden assumptions about timing.
A poorly designed test can defeat a sound hypothesis.
Recording predictions supports learning when cases are reviewed.
questions: If this explanation held, what should be observable tomorrow that is absent today?
What feature must remain stable for your prediction to follow?
Could a rival hypothesis predict exactly the same result?
What result are you prepared to count as evidence against your idea?
How would you test the prediction without quietly changing the outcome definition?
What would you predict if the same process started at a different time?
Did your test have a realistic opportunity to reveal the expected difference?
If the prediction fails, which supporting assumption could be checked independently?
If the prediction succeeds, which competing hypothesis survives that success?
What second prediction would distinguish the surviving accounts more sharply?

name: Causal reasoning
definition: Assess whether changing one factor would change an outcome, considering timing, alternative causes and how the observations were generated.
medicine: Doctors interpret associations in research and clinical records. Decisions about a modifiable factor depend on whether it has an effect in the relevant circumstances.
benefits: Identify a shared cause of exposure and outcome.
Recognise that worsening illness may influence which intervention a patient receives.
Explain why a group comparison might predict an outcome yet mislead about an intervention.
reasons: Association can survive adjustment while confounding remains.
Selecting only tested patients can create misleading patterns.
Reverse direction can produce the same association.
Effects can differ across populations and circumstances.
Distinguishing causes from predictors changes which clinical questions a study can answer.
questions: What exactly would be changed, for whom and over what interval?
Does the proposed cause precede the relevant change in the outcome?
Which factor could independently increase both the exposure and the outcome?
Could the patients' early deterioration have influenced the decision you call the exposure?
Who entered the dataset and how might that selection create the association?
Which variable might lie on the pathway through which the effect operates?
What comparison would make the exposed and unexposed groups more alike at the start?
What observation would distinguish a causal effect from a shared background trend?
What would you expect in a setting where the proposed pathway is unavailable?
Which causal claim still survives if the measurement of initial severity is incomplete?

name: Root-cause analysis
definition: Reconstruct an adverse event and investigate the interacting conditions, decisions and failed safeguards that made it possible.
medicine: A clinical incident often emerges at the intersection of people, equipment and workflow. Examining that intersection can reveal changes that prevent recurrence.
benefits: Reconstruct how an abnormal result reached the wrong inbox.
Identify which handover step allowed an unresolved task to disappear.
Propose a process change and a way to detect recurrence.
reasons: Stopping at the final mistake can leave its enabling conditions untouched.
Retrospect makes warning signs appear clearer than they were.
Different pathways can produce apparently identical incidents.
Local fixes can transfer risk to another team.
Near misses reveal safeguards that sometimes work and sometimes fail.
questions: Where does the last directly observed event end and retrospective interpretation begin?
What made the action reasonable to the person who took it at the time?
Which pre-existing condition allowed one error to reach the patient?
When the same error happened previously without harm, what interrupted it?
Was a safeguard missing, unusable, bypassed or never triggered?
Who inherited the task at the point where ownership became unclear?
What interacting changes would explain why the incident happened on this shift?
Which proposed fix would still work when staff are tired or information is incomplete?
Where could the fix simply move the bottleneck or the risk?
Which future observation would show that the underlying failure recurs despite fewer reports?

name: Mechanistic reasoning
definition: Explain an outcome by tracing how components and processes produce it under stated conditions.
medicine: A physiological mechanism links observations that otherwise look disconnected and helps a doctor anticipate what else should change when one link fails.
benefits: Connect a clinical sign to an intermediate physiological process.
Locate a break in a proposed pathway.
Explain why similar outward findings can arise through different processes.
reasons: A memorised association can fail outside its usual setting.
Feedback can mask the first disturbance.
Two pathways may converge on the same observable sign.
A mechanism that contradicts timing or scale needs revision.
A plausible pathway alone cannot establish how often an effect occurs in patients.
questions: What physical or biological step connects the proposed cause to the finding?
Which intermediate change should occur first?
What must be transported, transformed or sensed at each link?
Which link could fail while everything upstream remains intact?
Could a compensatory response hide the original disturbance?
Is the proposed mechanism fast enough to explain the observed onset?
Which other pathway reaches the same endpoint through a different intermediate?
What measurement would separate the two pathways most directly?
Is a mechanism established in one tissue plausible in the tissue involved here?
What empirical observation would you still need before treating this explanation as clinically important?

name: Forensic reasoning
definition: Reconstruct a past event from traces, records and testimony while keeping competing sequences and source limitations explicit.
medicine: Clinical teams often need to establish what happened during an unwitnessed episode or a fragmented handover, even when certainty remains limited.
benefits: Reconcile a sequence across ambulance and hospital records.
Separate a device's measurement time from the note's entry time.
State which aspects of an unwitnessed event cannot be reconstructed.
reasons: Contemporaneous and copied accounts carry different information.
Clock drift can reverse an apparent sequence.
Missing records can have mundane causes.
Recall can change after witnesses hear other accounts.
Responsible documentation preserves uncertainty for later reviewers.
questions: Which traces were created during the event and which were created afterwards?
What does the timestamp mark: observation, entry, upload or later amendment?
Which witness had direct access to the feature being described?
Could two similar accounts derive from a common handover?
Which part of your sequence depends on clocks being synchronised?
Could the gap in the record reflect a workflow interruption?
What alternate sequence yields the same surviving traces?
Which physical or documentary trace would discriminate between the sequences?
What can you say about timing without assigning an exact minute?
How would you distinguish observation, inference and unresolved uncertainty in your account?

name: Evidential reasoning
definition: Judge what information supports a claim by examining its relevance, provenance, independence, reliability and limitations.
medicine: A compelling-looking record may add little if it repeats an earlier source, measures a proxy or comes from a selected group.
benefits: Trace a reported finding back to its original observation.
Identify corroboration that comes from genuinely independent sources.
Explain which uncertainty an additional result actually reduces.
reasons: Copied findings can imitate agreement.
Measurements can be precise yet answer the wrong question.
Missingness may depend on illness severity.
A source can be reliable on one claim and weak on another.
Conflicting evidence often reveals an unexamined difference in context.
questions: What exact claim does this item support and how directly?
Who produced the information and what could they actually observe?
If you removed every copied note, how many observations would remain?
Could the same process have introduced error into all the agreeing measurements?
What did the instrument measure and how closely does that track the clinical question?
Whose information was most likely to go missing from this sample?
What feature would make this source less trustworthy for this specific claim?
Do the apparently opposing reports refer to the same time, population and definition?
What new evidence could change the balance independently of what you already have?
How far can you go before your conclusion outruns the evidence?

name: Bayesian reasoning
definition: Update the relative plausibility of explanations by combining starting odds with how differently each explanation predicts the new evidence.
medicine: Clinical findings have meaning in light of the patient's starting probability and the chance of seeing the same finding under alternatives.
benefits: Estimate how a result changes the odds of a diagnosis.
Explain why identical results can imply different risks in two settings.
Avoid counting a correlated pair of observations as independent evidence.
reasons: Base-rate neglect exaggerates uncommon explanations.
Confusing the probability of a result with the probability of disease reverses the question.
Evidence that fits every candidate may barely change the ranking.
Dependent findings can generate overconfident updates.
Decisions can require a different degree of certainty from explanations.
questions: What was a defensible starting probability before this result was known?
In which reference population would that starting probability be appropriate?
How often would you see this result if the leading explanation were true?
How often would you see it under the strongest alternative?
If both explanations predict the finding equally well, what happens to their odds?
If the starting odds are 1 to 9 and the evidence triples them, what probability follows?
Which observations arose from the same underlying event and might be double-counted?
How would your answer change if the result came from a population with a lower starting risk?
Can you explain the update using counts of people as well as probabilities?
How much uncertainty in the starting odds would change the decision you are considering?

name: Deductive reasoning
definition: Derive a conclusion that must hold if the stated premises are true and the inference is valid.
medicine: Clinical rules and research definitions support firm conclusions only within their assumptions. Following the logic exposes exactly where uncertainty enters.
benefits: Check whether a trial participant meets all stated inclusion criteria.
Identify the unstated premise behind a clinical claim.
Construct a counterexample to a conclusion that sounds inevitable.
reasons: A true conclusion can arise from invalid reasoning.
A valid inference can start from an inaccurate premise.
Necessary and sufficient conditions are easily confused.
Changes in definitions can invalidate an otherwise sound chain.
Showing the exact inferential step makes multidisciplinary review productive.
questions: Could every premise hold while your conclusion is false?
Which premise carries the greatest burden in this argument?
Is the rule stated for every member of a group or only for most?
Where has a probable observation quietly become a certainty?
Would the reverse implication also follow, and what case would test it?
Which patient would satisfy the first two requirements but violate the third?
Has the meaning of a key term changed between premise and conclusion?
What is the weakest conclusion the premises guarantee?
Which single additional premise would justify the stronger claim?
If the argument is valid but conflicts with an observation, which premise can you verify independently?

name: Inductive reasoning
definition: Infer a provisional general pattern from a set of observations and judge how far it can extend to new cases.
medicine: Experience becomes clinically useful when a doctor learns a regularity while recognising the population, setting and exceptions that constrain it.
benefits: Formulate a pattern across repeated presentations.
Check whether a clinic-based observation generalises to primary care.
Revise a teaching rule when a new case reveals its boundary.
reasons: Convenient samples can hide important subgroups.
Rare exceptions may matter clinically.
Repeated observations from one patient offer less breadth than independent cases.
A seasonal or service change can imitate a stable pattern.
Testing a generalisation on fresh cases limits hindsight.
questions: What feature recurs across independently observed cases?
Which kinds of patients had no opportunity to appear in your sample?
Are twenty encounters with the same patient evidence about twenty different people?
Does the pattern survive when you change the observer or the clinic?
Is the group defined in a way that already guarantees your apparent discovery?
Which exception would narrow the rule without destroying its useful part?
What case is most unlike the originals while still falling within your proposed scope?
What prediction can you write down before you see the next case?
Which background change might have made a temporary trend look universal?
How would you describe your generalisation so a colleague knows where caution begins?

name: Syllogistic reasoning
definition: Test whether a conclusion about categories follows from two linked premises and their quantifiers, such as all, some or none.
medicine: Clinical classifications and eligibility criteria often use nested categories. A change from some to all can alter who appears to qualify.
benefits: Check category membership against a study definition.
Spot an invalid overlap claim in a referral rule.
Explain what a subgroup finding establishes about an individual.
reasons: A shared property can falsely suggest identical groups.
Subgroup and whole-group claims often use different quantifiers.
An everyday term may denote different classes across two policies.
Negation can attach to the wrong part of a statement.
A diagram can expose a counterexample that fluent prose disguises.
questions: Which three categories appear in this argument?
Does the middle category mean exactly the same thing in both premises?
If every member of A belongs to B, must every member of B belong to A?
If some members of B qualify, what else would establish that someone in A qualifies?
Could two patient groups share one sign yet have no patients in common?
Where does the claim change from some patients to every patient?
If no member of one group has a feature, what follows for its subgroups?
Does the wording establish that the category contains any patients at all?
Can you draw the smallest arrangement of overlapping groups that defeats the conclusion?
Which revision to a premise would make the proposed conclusion follow?

name: Conditional reasoning
definition: Work through the implications of if–then statements while distinguishing necessary conditions, sufficient conditions and exceptions.
medicine: Protocols, safety nets and decision rules depend on exactly which condition triggers a conclusion and what can be inferred when it is absent.
benefits: Interpret the trigger in a review protocol.
Identify when an observation satisfies only one condition in a multistep rule.
Explain why a recorded action may have occurred through another route.
reasons: Everyday if–then language often hides exceptions.
Reversing a conditional can create an unwarranted diagnosis.
Missing information creates a third practical state beyond present or absent.
Multiple triggers can produce the same action.
A rule's scope can expire when the clinical setting changes.
questions: Is the stated condition sufficient, necessary or both for the outcome?
What must be true before this rule even applies?
If several triggers can prompt a review, what can you infer from seeing a review documented?
Which case would meet the trigger yet lack the stated consequence?
If the trigger is unrecorded, can you treat it as absent?
How does the meaning change between if A and B, and if A or B?
Under a genuinely exceptionless rule, what follows when the consequence is absent?
Does the rule describe an obligation to act or a prediction about what actually happens?
Which exception would turn a seemingly contradictory case into an expected one?
How would you restate the rule so a colleague could tell exactly when to apply it?

name: Transitive reasoning
definition: Infer a relation between endpoints through a common middle term when that particular relation supports chaining.
medicine: Ordering events, comparing measurements and navigating nested classifications often require valid chains. Many familiar clinical relationships do not support such a chain.
benefits: Reconstruct event order from partial timestamps.
Infer an endpoint comparison on a common measurement scale.
Recognise when a chain of associations cannot justify a direct association.
reasons: Measurements taken under different conditions can break a chain.
Approximately equal is a poor basis for exact ordering.
Similarity need not extend through a common example.
Mixed directions make seemingly neat chains inconclusive.
Identical labels can hide different reference groups.
questions: What is the precise relation connecting the first pair and the second pair?
If A occurred before B and B before C, what is established about A and C?
If A resembles B and B resembles C, what would justify the same conclusion about A and C?
Do both statements refer to the same middle event or only to similarly named events?
Are all three measurements expressed on the same scale and under comparable conditions?
How does rounding affect a chain of apparently equal values?
What can you infer if each endpoint comes before the middle event?
If one timestamp is an interval, which endpoint ordering is still forced?
Could A be associated with B and B with C while A and C are unrelated?
What smallest change to one link makes the endpoint conclusion undecidable?

name: Disjunctive reasoning
definition: Evaluate alternatives connected by or, checking whether the options are exhaustive and whether more than one may hold.
medicine: Clinical classifications, explanations and workflow decisions frequently offer alternatives whose boundaries can overlap or leave out a third possibility.
benefits: Clarify whether a criterion accepts either or both findings.
Notice a false choice between two potentially coexisting processes.
Determine what an exclusion establishes in a genuinely exhaustive set.
reasons: Everyday wording can conceal whether options are exclusive.
A leftover category may contain several explanations.
Negative evidence varies in whether it really removes an option.
Coexisting conditions require a different interpretation from alternatives.
Decision forms can force choices more narrowly than the evidence permits.
questions: What exactly does or allow in this case: either one, both, or exactly one?
Who established that the offered options exhaust the possibilities?
Could both proposed processes explain different parts of the same presentation?
If one option becomes less likely, what justifies treating it as eliminated?
What third possibility would make your apparent choice premature?
If one alternative is established, when does the other still need checking?
Does the form require a single answer even though the underlying state permits two?
Which observation could identify both alternatives occurring together?
If neither category fits, is there a missing case or a mistaken definition?
What conclusion follows after one option is excluded, and which premise makes it follow?

name: Contradiction-based reasoning
definition: Temporarily accept a claim and trace its implications until an inconsistency reveals that some premise, definition or inference needs revision.
medicine: Contradictions in clinical timelines and models can expose an error, provided the doctor checks which statements really conflict and which source warrants revision.
benefits: Identify mutually impossible timestamps.
Test a proposed mechanism against a constraint it must obey.
Reconcile conflicting claims before carrying either into a discharge summary.
reasons: A seeming conflict may reflect different times or definitions.
The contradiction alone rarely identifies the incorrect premise.
Discomfort with an unusual result can masquerade as logical impossibility.
Assuming an unreliable instrument is perfect can misplace blame.
Resolving conflicts explicitly prevents silent propagation of errors.
questions: What follows if you temporarily assume the disputed claim is true?
Which exact pair of its consequences cannot both hold?
Could the conflicting statements describe different moments in time?
Do the two sources use the same meaning of normal, recent or first?
Is the result genuinely impossible or simply improbable?
What hidden assumption about the instrument creates the inconsistency?
If either of two premises could be wrong, what evidence distinguishes them?
Can you remove one assumption and make every observation cohere?
What must be abandoned, and what remains intact after the contradiction?
How would you record an unresolved inconsistency without choosing a winner by convenience?

name: Recursive reasoning
definition: Solve a problem by applying the same rule to smaller instances or to a preceding state, with a base case or stopping condition.
medicine: Some clinical and administrative structures repeat at successive levels. A sound rule lets a doctor trace nested records, family relationships or serial model states without losing the starting assumptions.
benefits: Trace a family relationship through successive generations.
Unpack a nested referral chain to its originating observation.
Check whether a recurrence for daily totals handles its first day correctly.
reasons: An incorrect starting value contaminates later results.
A circular reference can keep a process running indefinitely.
Repeated application can amplify small errors.
A rule that works on one level may fail at a boundary.
Independent small examples make an opaque iterative calculation auditable.
questions: What is the smallest version of this problem you can answer directly?
How does the answer at one stage depend on a previous or smaller stage?
What must decrease or change so that following the rule eventually ends?
What happens on the first day, when there is no previous daily total?
Can a referral point back to a record already visited?
If a branch has no children, what value should it contribute?
How would an erroneous starting value propagate after three applications?
Does the rule still work when two branches share an ancestor?
Can you solve a three-level example independently and compare the answers?
What clinical meaning disappears if the calculation returns only a final value?

name: Combinatorial reasoning
definition: Enumerate possible selections, arrangements or joint states while accounting for order, overlap and constraints.
medicine: The number of possible combinations of findings, samples or staff assignments grows quickly. Systematic counting exposes missing cases and mistaken denominators.
benefits: List the distinct patterns of several binary findings.
Check whether a sampling plan covers relevant combinations.
Count feasible allocations while preventing accidental double-counting.
reasons: Order matters for some clinical sequences and not for others.
Mutually exclusive options change counts.
Distinct labels can describe the same underlying case.
Possibility does not imply equal probability.
Efficient grouping makes large spaces easier to audit.
questions: Which elements can vary independently and which combinations are impossible?
Does reversing the order create a new clinical sequence or the same group?
How many possible presence-or-absence patterns exist for three findings before constraints?
What happens to the count if two findings can never coexist by definition?
Can you partition the possibilities so each case belongs to exactly one group?
Where might two descriptions be counting the same patient twice?
Which rare combination is missing from the way you sampled cases?
Why might two equally numerous groups have very different probabilities?
How could you use symmetry to simplify the count while preserving meaningful differences?
Can a second counting method reproduce your total or expose an omission?

name: Constraint-based reasoning
definition: Find which solutions are possible when all stated restrictions must hold simultaneously, and test whether the solution is unique.
medicine: Clinical scheduling, record reconstruction and diagnostic puzzles can have several plausible answers until their restrictions are considered together.
benefits: Detect incompatible requirements in a follow-up plan.
Narrow a possible timeline using several independent observations.
Explain when an assignment has multiple equally valid solutions.
reasons: Satisfying every constraint separately can still fail to satisfy them jointly.
Some restrictions are negotiable preferences.
A newly added condition can invalidate earlier work.
A single feasible answer gives no proof of uniqueness.
Infeasibility can identify contradictory requirements rather than poor effort.
questions: Which conditions are mandatory and which are preferences you could revisit?
What does each restriction remove from the set of possible answers?
Can you build an example satisfying each pair of conditions but failing the whole set?
Which time window constrains the sequence most tightly?
If you reorder the restrictions, do you reach the same feasible set?
What second allocation survives every requirement you have stated?
If no solution exists, which smallest group of requirements causes the conflict?
What extra observation would distinguish the remaining feasible timelines?
Which constraint came from the patient's circumstances and which from your own assumption?
How would you show a colleague that a solution remains possible after one requirement changes?

name: Analogical reasoning
definition: Map corresponding roles and relationships between two situations and examine which inferences survive that mapping.
medicine: A well-chosen comparison can explain unfamiliar physiology or a care process. Its value depends on matching the relevant dependency and identifying where the correspondence fails.
benefits: Explain a limiting step through a familiar queue.
Transfer a useful insight between two clinical workflows.
Identify where an educational analogy would generate a false prediction.
reasons: Surface resemblance can hide opposite causal directions.
One element in the source may lack a counterpart in the target.
A useful analogy can fail when the operating range changes.
A strong comparison generates a checkable target prediction.
Explicit limits protect patients from misleading explanations.
questions: Which role does each element in the first system play in the second?
What dependency links the matched roles?
If you rename every object, can you still describe what the cases share?
Which aspect of the source has no defensible clinical counterpart?
Does the relationship run in the same direction in both situations?
What novel prediction follows for the target if the mapping holds?
Could a different comparison fit the surface equally well yet predict the opposite?
Where would the source's behaviour change while the target's stays stable?
What example would preserve the vocabulary while breaking the relationship?
How could you explain the comparison's useful range to a patient in one sentence?

name: Anomalous reasoning
definition: Identify a departure from an expected pattern, establish that the comparison is fair and investigate what the discrepancy reveals.
medicine: An unexpected trajectory can expose an overlooked process, a faulty measurement or an unsuitable baseline. The first task is to establish what is genuinely surprising.
benefits: Notice a result incompatible with its prior trajectory.
Separate a real service change from a reporting change.
Investigate a discrepant clue before averaging it away.
reasons: Population ranges and an individual's usual values can diverge.
Rare observations occur by chance in large sets.
Instrument changes can mimic physiology.
A single outlier can reveal an overlooked subgroup.
Both overreacting to noise and discarding exceptions obscure useful signals.
questions: Against which baseline is this observation unusual?
Would it remain unusual for this individual at this time of day?
How many measurements offered a chance for one striking outlier to appear?
Did the device, sample handling or reporting method change?
Is the size of the deviation large relative to ordinary variation?
Does a second, independent observation reproduce the unexpected feature?
Could the observation belong to a subgroup with a different expected pattern?
Which existing explanation predicts the exception rather than merely tolerating it?
When would excluding this point erase the most informative part of the dataset?
What future pattern would make you revise the baseline itself?

name: Antinomic reasoning
definition: Identify rules or claims that yield mutually incompatible requirements under the same conditions and examine the assumptions responsible.
medicine: Conflicting protocols or definitions can make an apparently straightforward clinical workflow impossible. Naming the conflict helps a team seek clarification about scope or priority.
benefits: Identify two recording rules that require incompatible entries.
Show why two eligibility definitions classify the same case differently.
Ask who can resolve a conflict between simultaneous duties.
reasons: A disagreement can disappear when scopes are clarified.
Apparent compliance may conceal an impossible requirement.
Changing a single definition may reconcile the rules.
Preserving both arguments makes escalation more informative.
Distinguishing a genuine conflict from an inconvenient trade-off protects scarce attention.
questions: What does each rule require in this specific case?
Can both requirements hold at the same time under the same definitions?
Is the conflict in the facts, in the rules or in a hidden assumption?
Do the rules govern the same person, setting and time interval?
Can you construct the smallest realistic case that triggers both?
Would narrowing either rule's scope remove the inconsistency?
What legitimate purpose would be lost if you simply discarded one rule?
Does a stated priority or exception already resolve the conflict?
What information would clarify the contradiction, and what requires a value judgment?
How would you describe the unresolved pair so a colleague can verify it independently?

name: Antithetical reasoning
definition: Examine two opposing relationships, positions or tendencies and identify the dimension along which they oppose each other.
medicine: Clinical aims can pull in opposing directions, and a contrast can clarify the conditions in which each tendency matters most.
benefits: Explain how a lower decision threshold can increase detection and false alarms together.
Contrast opposing physiological influences on an outcome.
Present the strongest case for two rival priorities in planning care.
reasons: Opposites can coexist in the same system.
Opposing positions can rely on different time horizons.
Reversing one conclusion may fail to produce its genuine alternative.
The balance can shift across patient circumstances.
Making the axis of opposition explicit can reveal shared goals.
questions: Along which single dimension do these two positions actually point in opposite directions?
Does the opposition concern goals, mechanisms, measurements or values?
Could both tendencies operate at once even though they push the outcome in different directions?
What would tip the balance towards one tendency?
Does reversing the sign of the model correspond to a meaningful clinical opposite?
Could short-term and long-term outcomes make the two positions look further apart?
Which evidence would strengthen one position while weakening the other?
What do the strongest advocates on each side agree about?
Is the apparent opposition hiding a third option on a different dimension?
When would describing the positions as exact opposites distort the patient's choices?

name: Higher-order relational reasoning
definition: Compare or combine relationships themselves, such as judging whether one factor changes the strength or direction of another relationship.
medicine: Many clinical questions concern a dependency that changes with context. Comparing relationships can expose effect modification and prevent misleading summaries.
benefits: Ask whether a marker's relation to an outcome varies across groups.
Compare how workload influences delays in two services.
Distinguish an average difference from a difference in how quickly two measures change together.
reasons: Group averages can conceal different underlying slopes.
Apparent interaction can depend on the chosen scale.
A third variable can change more than the baseline level.
Unequal observation ranges can imitate a relationship difference.
Explicit comparisons help doctors state which dependency their conclusion concerns.
questions: Are you comparing two values or the relationships between two pairs of values?
Could two groups share an average yet differ in how steeply the outcome changes?
What third factor might change the effect of the first on the second?
Does the apparent difference persist on both absolute and relative scales?
Are the ranges of the predictor comparable in the groups?
What does it mean if two curves cross instead of remaining parallel?
Could unequal measurement precision create apparently different slopes?
What evidence would distinguish a change in baseline from a change in dependency?
Which part of a relationship between relationships must survive in a cross-domain comparison?
What prediction for a new group follows from your proposed interaction?

name: Cross-domain reasoning
definition: Carry a principle, representation or method from one field into another and verify how the receiving field constrains its use.
medicine: Doctors borrow ideas from engineering, statistics and the social sciences. Applying them responsibly requires checking what the imported terms mean in the clinical setting.
benefits: Use queueing concepts to examine a clinic bottleneck.
Translate a physical flow model into a question about volume balance.
Test whether a method from one specialty retains meaning in another.
reasons: A shared word can denote different quantities.
Assumptions familiar in one field may be violated in medicine.
The unit of analysis may change during transfer.
A borrowed method can reveal a previously unmeasured variable.
Validation in the receiving setting helps distinguish insight from a persuasive metaphor.
questions: Which result from another field are you trying to carry across?
What does each variable mean in the original domain and here?
Which assumptions does a specialist in the source field take for granted?
What plays the role of an arrival, departure or bottleneck in this clinic?
Does the receiving domain have feedback absent from the source model?
Where could a word such as resistance conceal two different measurements?
What would the borrowed principle predict that clinical intuition alone did not?
Which measurable outcome could test that prediction in the receiving setting?
Would a change in scale from an organ to a hospital undermine the transfer?
After adaptation, which part of the original principle is still doing explanatory work?

name: Abstract reasoning
definition: Represent the essential relationships of a problem in a form that remains useful when particular names and surface details change.
medicine: A doctor can recognise shared structure across presentations or study designs while preserving the details that affect the validity of a conclusion.
benefits: Represent repeated measurements as a trajectory.
Recognise the same confounding pattern across studies involving different exposures.
Summarise a case in terms that support a transferable question.
reasons: Overly broad summaries erase clinically decisive differences.
Excessive detail prevents recognition of a common structure.
The same case can support several useful levels of description.
A good abstraction makes predictions possible on an unseen case.
Knowing how to reintroduce detail protects individualised judgment.
questions: Which features could change without changing the logic of this case?
What is the simplest representation that still supports the intended inference?
If you remove every disease name, what roles and dependencies remain?
Which patient detail looks superficial but would reverse the conclusion?
Can two very different stories instantiate the same structure?
Can two similar stories demand different structures?
Would a graph, equation or verbal rule best preserve the relevant distinction?
What new case does your abstraction allow you to solve?
Which boundary case shows that your model has become too general?
How would you put the omitted detail back when moving from a teaching example to an individual patient?

name: Hierarchical reasoning
definition: Reasoning across nested levels of organisation or classification while keeping track of which claims belong at each level.
medicine: A doctor moves between a person's findings, an organ system, a tissue and a cellular process. Evidence at one level can narrow the possibilities at another while leaving important exceptions.
benefits: Locate the level at which an explanation still leaves a clinical finding unexplained.
Translate a molecular finding into a question about function that matters to the patient.
Organise a broad differential into branches that can be narrowed with evidence.
reasons: Broad labels can hide important differences between subtypes.
A finding in a tissue sample may describe only part of an organ.
A hospital average can conceal clinically important variation between wards.
Two findings that sit under one parent category may arise by different routes.
Moving back to the whole patient can expose a cost invisible at the cellular level.
questions: A tissue sample is abnormal. What extra evidence would justify a claim about the whole organ?
Two disorders share a parent category. Which inference can you carry from one to the other, and which needs fresh evidence?
A ward reports fewer falls while the hospital reports more. How could both observations be accurate?
At what level would you look for a single explanation of several apparently unrelated findings?
Which patient-level outcome would show that a change seen in cells actually matters?
How would you choose the next branch of a diagnostic tree if two labels overlap?
Which distinction disappears when you group these cases under a broader heading?
If a hospital policy appears ineffective, how would you tell whether the difficulty lies in its design or in one ward's implementation?
Which features justify subdividing a familiar category, and would that division change a decision?
What observation would make you abandon your chosen level of explanation and move up or down a level?

name: Spatial reasoning
definition: Inferring how objects, surfaces and spaces relate when a viewpoint, orientation or section changes.
medicine: Images, drawings and examination findings often describe the same anatomy from different viewpoints. A doctor must align the views before deciding which structures could be involved.
benefits: Build a three-dimensional account from neighbouring image slices.
Describe the position of a finding using a shared anatomical reference frame.
Check whether a suspected location could account for the distribution of observed signs.
reasons: A change of viewpoint can make a fixed structure seem to move.
A mirror image and a rotation can look deceptively similar.
One slice can hide continuity that becomes apparent on adjacent slices.
Left and right can be miscommunicated when observers face opposite ways.
Knowing which structures could touch can rule out an otherwise plausible account.
questions: After the image is rotated through 180 degrees, which structures remain adjacent even though their positions on the screen have changed?
Two round profiles appear on a single slice. What could show whether they belong to one folded tube or two separate tubes?
Which landmarks let you align two images taken with the patient in different positions?
What feature would distinguish a mirrored view from a rotated view of the same asymmetric structure?
A finding appears above a landmark on the screen. What do you need to know before calling it anatomically superior?
Which neighbouring slice would most clearly distinguish your two proposed shapes?
How could an oblique cut produce an ellipse through a circular structure?
Where would you expect a continuous tract to reappear if your reconstruction is correct?
What additional viewpoint would resolve an ambiguity that repeated inspection of this image cannot?
How would you describe the location to a colleague who cannot see the picture or your gestures?

name: Temporal reasoning
definition: Using sequence, duration, interval and change of pace to constrain what could have happened.
medicine: An episode's course may distinguish explanations that produce the same findings at a single visit. A timeline also reveals what the record leaves uncertain.
benefits: Reconcile symptom onset with when each observation was actually made.
Separate a recurring episode from a continuously changing course.
Reconstruct a handover timeline from observations with different time stamps.
reasons: The first documented sign may occur long after the first symptom.
Irregular sampling can make gradual change appear sudden.
Different clocks or delayed chart entries can reverse an apparent sequence.
Duration and recurrence can distinguish otherwise similar histories.
A disputed time point can determine whether an explanation is even possible.
questions: When was the finding first present, and when did someone first have an opportunity to notice it?
How would your account change if a note's time marked when it was entered rather than when the event occurred?
Two readings are six hours apart. What changes between them remain compatible with both values?
Which proposed cause is impossible under every ordering consistent with the records?
What question would turn “it happened recently” into an interval you can actually use?
Which event is the best independent anchor when two observers' clocks disagree?
How would you distinguish three brief episodes from one continuous episode with three observations?
If a symptom preceded an exposure, what causal stories are still open to you?
Which matters more for distinguishing the two accounts here: the order, the delay or the duration?
What new observation would shrink the uncertainty about the sequence most?

name: Structural reasoning
definition: Identifying how parts are connected and determining what those connections enable or constrain.
medicine: Anatomical pathways and clinical services depend on their arrangement. Two systems with the same parts can behave differently when the connections change.
benefits: Identify a shared junction that could link several downstream findings.
Trace how a referral reaches the team responsible for action.
Distinguish genuine backup arrangements from two routes dependent on a single component.
reasons: An inventory of parts can overlook a critical missing connection.
Apparent redundancy can disappear when two routes share a bottleneck.
Location can explain why disruption of one small link has wide consequences.
A useful diagram exposes assumptions about direction and access.
Comparing arrangements can reveal a solution that adding more parts would miss.
questions: Two services have identical staff and equipment. Which difference in their connections could explain unequal outcomes?
If one junction were unavailable, which parts of the pathway could still communicate?
What evidence shows that the arrow in your diagram represents a real transfer of information?
Two downstream functions fail together. Which shared upstream link is worth examining?
How could you distinguish two independent backup routes from two routes sharing a hidden dependency?
Which change in the arrangement would alter function even if every component stayed intact?
Where can information enter this system without ever reaching the person who must act?
Which part sits next to the problem yet plays no role in its route through the system?
What finding would force you to redraw a connection rather than add another component?
What is the smallest diagram that preserves every dependency needed to explain the outcome?

name: Semantic reasoning
definition: Inferring meaning by examining how a word, concept or category is used in context.
medicine: Patients, clinicians and forms can use the same word for different experiences. Clarifying its meaning can change what evidence a doctor should seek.
benefits: Translate an everyday symptom word into a description the patient recognises.
Check whether a study's outcome label matches the outcome a patient cares about.
Detect when two teams document the same term using different operational definitions.
reasons: Familiar words can conceal disagreement about the underlying experience.
A changed definition can create an apparent trend without a change in illness.
A broader label can alter who qualifies for a study or service.
A patient's metaphor can convey information lost in a technical paraphrase.
Precise terms make clinical uncertainty easier to communicate.
questions: When a patient says “dizzy”, what example from their own experience would clarify the word?
Two clinicians agree that someone is “stable”. What distinct claims might each be making?
Which part of a patient's description would be lost if you replaced it with a familiar diagnostic label?
A study reports “recovery”. What would you inspect before relating that result to the patient's goal?
Could two apparently conflicting reports become consistent under one explicit definition?
How would a changed case definition alter who enters the denominator of an audit?
Which words in this handover describe an observation, and which already contain an interpretation?
What borderline case would expose disagreement about where a category ends?
A patient repeats your words back accurately. How could you check whether you mean the same thing?
Which paraphrase preserves the patient's intended meaning while remaining useful to the next clinician?

name: Probabilistic reasoning
definition: Representing uncertainty and combining available information to judge how plausible alternative outcomes are.
medicine: Doctors make decisions before outcomes are known. A defensible probability judgment specifies the event, the relevant population and the evidence available at that moment.
benefits: Explain uncertainty using counts in a relevant comparison group.
Compare rare but plausible explanations with common alternatives.
Recognise when several observations depend on the same underlying process.
reasons: A probability has little meaning without a defined outcome and time period.
The denominator can change the interpretation of an apparently striking event.
Dependent signs can create unjustified confidence when counted separately.
Small samples can produce runs and clusters by chance.
A plausible range can communicate limited knowledge more honestly than a precise figure.
questions: What event exactly are you assigning a chance to, over what period and for whom?
Out of 100 comparable people, what counts would make your verbal estimate accurate?
Which comparison group best resembles this patient on the features that matter?
Two signs often occur together. How would their dependence change the weight you give the pair?
What would have to be true for a surprising cluster to be compatible with chance?
If the common explanation and a rare explanation both fit this clue, what else should affect their ranking?
Which uncertainty would shrink with another observation, and which reflects genuine variation between people?
How could two clinicians quote different risks while agreeing on all the underlying counts?
What range of probabilities could you defend if the denominator were only approximately known?
Which event is more likely to happen first, and how would that change the chance of observing the other?

name: Statistical reasoning
definition: Drawing conclusions about populations and differences from sampled data while accounting for variability, selection and uncertainty.
medicine: Clinical research and service audits are samples produced by particular measurement processes. Their numbers acquire clinical meaning through the choices that generated them.
benefits: Assess whether a study sample supports a conclusion about a particular patient group.
Distinguish a potentially meaningful difference from imprecision in its estimate.
Check how missing observations or changed denominators affect audit results.
reasons: A large sample can preserve bias when selection is systematic.
A mean can obscure subgroups with very different experiences.
Repeated readings on one person do not provide independent observations from many people.
Excluding incomplete records can change the clinical question being answered.
Precision and clinical importance answer different questions.
questions: A service reports shorter average waits. Who had to remain in the dataset for that improvement to appear?
Which unit was sampled here: visits, people or clinics, and how would that affect uncertainty?
Two studies estimate the same effect with different intervals. What explains their different precision?
What distribution could have the reported mean while leaving many patients worse off?
Which missing patients would most threaten the conclusion if their outcomes differed?
How would you explain a narrow interval around a difference too small to matter to patients?
What variable might reverse the apparent association when data from different wards are pooled?
How would you tell a genuine change in the population from a change in who was measured?
What would an association measured only among clinic attendees tell you about those who never attended?
Which new sample would most sharply test whether this finding travels beyond the original setting?

name: Counterfactual reasoning
definition: Considering how the same case would have unfolded under a specified alternative to what actually happened.
medicine: Patients and clinicians often ask whether an outcome would have differed if an earlier event had changed. A careful answer separates the observed history from the assumptions needed to construct its alternative.
benefits: Examine whether recovery after an action supports a claim that the action caused it.
Anticipate how an incident might have unfolded with a functioning safeguard.
Explain why an individual's unobserved alternative outcome remains uncertain.
reasons: Improvement can occur along a natural course even after a memorable event.
Changing one earlier fact can alter several later events.
Comparisons can be biased when people receiving different care began with different risks.
Two causal models can fit the same history and predict different alternatives.
Explicit assumptions make a retrospective judgment fairer to the people involved.
questions: What precise event would you change in this history, and what would remain as it was immediately beforehand?
Which later events would also change as consequences of your imagined alternative?
A patient improved after an intervention. What evidence would help estimate the course without it?
Who would be a credible comparison for a person whose alternative outcome can never be observed?
Which assumption lets you use another person's experience to reason about this one?
If the suggested safeguard had worked, was there another route to the same outcome?
Can two explanations agree about everything observed yet disagree about what would have happened otherwise?
What would make a before-and-after comparison misleading in this particular case?
How would knowing only what was available at the time change your judgment of a past decision?
Which part of your alternative history can be checked, and which must remain conditional?

name: Hypothetical reasoning
definition: Exploring what follows if a premise is provisionally assumed, including premises whose truth remains undecided.
medicine: Clinical teams can rehearse several plausible situations before one materialises. Keeping each assumption visible prevents a possibility raised in discussion from becoming a recorded fact.
benefits: Explore the implications of an uncertain test finding before acting on it.
Construct contingency plans for different follow-up outcomes.
Probe the assumptions behind a colleague's proposed explanation.
reasons: A possible explanation can gain false authority through repetition.
Contrasting scenarios can expose which uncertainty matters to the next decision.
An impossible premise can make a logically coherent plan unusable.
A useful scenario specifies what could show it has become relevant.
Separating branch-specific consequences from shared ones simplifies planning.
questions: Suppose a surprising measurement is accurate. Which other observations would then become hard to explain?
What if the instrument were at fault instead: which of your conclusions would survive?
Which unverified assumption carries the greatest weight in this scenario?
Can your imagined situation occur under the constraints you have already accepted?
What observation would separate two possibilities that currently lead to the same plan?
If the assumed finding proves false tomorrow, which parts of today's plan could still be justified?
Which seemingly different scenarios make identical predictions within the available time?
How would you record an assumption clearly enough that a colleague could not mistake it for a confirmed fact?
Which additional assumption did you introduce between your opening premise and your final claim?
What is the simplest alternative scenario that exposes a weakness in the proposed plan?

name: Predictive reasoning
definition: Using a rule, model or pattern to make a checkable claim about a previously unobserved outcome.
medicine: Predictions help a doctor notice when a working account fails. Their value depends on a clear outcome, time horizon and comparison with what was later observed.
benefits: State what change a proposed mechanism predicts before reviewing the next observation.
Anticipate service demand over an explicit interval.
Audit whether a model's claimed probabilities match subsequent outcomes.
reasons: A vague forecast can appear correct under nearly any result.
A model can succeed by relying on a shortcut that disappears elsewhere.
Forecast accuracy can change when the population or measurement process changes.
The commonest outcome is an essential benchmark for a complex model.
Recorded predictions help distinguish genuine foresight from hindsight.
questions: What observable outcome and time window would make your forecast capable of being wrong?
What would the simplest forecast using only the usual frequency predict here?
Which input is available at the moment of prediction and which became known afterwards?
What result would count as a meaningful failure even if the average error stayed small?
A forecast performs well overall. In which group would a systematic error matter most?
How would a change in how clinicians detect the outcome affect apparent accuracy?
Which prediction differs most between your two proposed models?
If the forecast itself changes care, how might that alter what you later observe?
When outcomes assigned a one-in-five chance are followed up, what pattern would support those estimates?
What observation would show that the model needs revising rather than that an unlikely outcome occurred?

name: Prognostic reasoning
definition: Estimating the likely course, timing and range of outcomes of an existing health problem under specified circumstances.
medicine: Patients often want to know what living with an illness may look like. Prognosis connects evidence from comparable cases to their health, circumstances and priorities.
benefits: Discuss a range of possible trajectories using a time horizon meaningful to the patient.
Identify milestones that warrant revisiting an earlier estimate.
Distinguish prospects for survival, symptom relief and daily function.
reasons: People with the same diagnosis can follow different courses.
A population estimate becomes less useful when its starting point differs from the patient's.
An accurate prediction about survival may answer a different question from one about independence.
Other events can prevent the outcome of interest from being observed.
New information can make a once reasonable estimate obsolete.
questions: What future outcome does this person actually want to understand, and by when?
Does the reference group's clock start at symptom onset, diagnosis or another milestone?
Which features make the patients in the study better or worse comparisons for this person?
How might two people with the same label have different prospects for returning to daily activities?
What event could occur first and prevent observation of the outcome you are discussing?
How would the estimate change if the person has already remained well beyond an early high-risk period?
Which aspect of the expected course is sufficiently uncertain to express as a range?
What milestone would justify revisiting the estimate with the patient?
How might changes in available care limit the relevance of an older cohort?
How would you answer a question about time while preserving room for several plausible individual courses?

name: Extrapolative reasoning
definition: Extending an observed relationship beyond the range of times, values or populations in which it was established.
medicine: A clinical relationship observed over a narrow range may change when a biological limit, different population or new measurement regime is reached. The proposed extension needs an explicit boundary.
benefits: Interrogate forecasts that extend beyond the duration of follow-up.
Check whether a trend observed in one age range could apply in another.
Spot impossible values produced by a simple straight-line extension.
reasons: A straight line can conceal a threshold, plateau or reversal.
Short observation periods reveal little about delayed changes.
Groups outside a study can differ in mechanisms as well as starting risk.
Uncertainty can grow quickly beyond the measured range.
Identifying the first unsupported step guides collection of new evidence.
questions: Exactly where do the observed data end and your projected relationship begin?
What biological or practical boundary would your line eventually cross?
Could a straight line and a plateau fit the measured points equally well yet disagree later?
Which unmeasured group differs most from the people who established the original trend?
What mechanism would have to remain stable for the extension to hold?
How far could the prediction move before ordinary measurement error swamps the apparent trend?
Which new observation just outside the original range would best test the extension?
How would a change in background care alter a projection into later years?
What would doubling the projection distance do to your confidence, and why?
How would you communicate the difference between an observed benefit at one year and a projected benefit at five?

name: Proportional reasoning
definition: Relating quantities by ratios, rates and scale factors while keeping the numerator, denominator and units explicit.
medicine: Clinical comparisons often turn on the population, area, mass or duration to which a count relates. A well-chosen denominator can change the interpretation of the same numerator.
benefits: Translate a relative change into absolute counts for a stated baseline.
Compare event rates across groups with different observation periods.
Check whether a geometrical change scales a length, area or volume.
reasons: Identical relative changes can have very different absolute consequences.
Ratios built from different denominators can sound comparable.
An average of subgroup rates can misrepresent the combined population.
Doubling a length need not double a volume.
An assumed proportional relationship can break when a process saturates.
questions: Relative to what quantity is this measurement being expressed?
A risk falls from two in a hundred to one in a hundred. How could two accurate descriptions leave different impressions?
Two wards count the same number of events. What denominators would make a comparison fair?
When does combining two group rates require weighting by their different sizes?
Which quantities must stay fixed before doubling one quantity should double another?
If an image is magnified, which measurements scale with length and which with area?
What units remain after you divide these two quantities, and do those units answer the question?
Could a high rate in a small group coexist with most events arising in a lower-rate group?
What pattern in the data would show that a ratio you treated as constant actually changes with scale?
What denominator would make this finding most meaningful to the person affected?

name: Mathematical reasoning
definition: Choosing quantities and assumptions, expressing their relationships precisely and deriving consequences that can be checked.
medicine: A doctor can use equations or formal models to establish exactly what the observations determine. Writing down the unknowns often reveals why a numerical answer would be unjustified.
benefits: Build a balance equation linking inflow, outflow and observed change.
Check whether a reported result has units compatible with its interpretation.
Identify assumptions that make a clinical estimate sensitive to small errors.
reasons: A mathematically valid calculation can still answer the wrong clinical question.
More unknowns than independent constraints can leave multiple valid explanations.
Checking extreme cases can expose a model that behaves implausibly.
Changing how a quantity is represented can reveal a simpler invariant.
An explicit model makes a hidden assumption available for challenge.
questions: Which quantities are observed and which are parameters you would need to infer?
What balance or conservation principle could relate these variables?
A compartment grows by one litre per minute. What else would you need to determine its inflow?
What units should your predicted value have, and which factor could account for a mismatch?
Are all of your equations independent, or have you written the same constraint twice?
What happens to the result when one input approaches zero?
Can two different sets of parameter values reproduce every observation you currently have?
Which measurement error would change the conclusion most if you propagated it through the model?
What simpler representation preserves the feature that matters to the patient?
Which observed result would show that the equation describes the wrong process?

name: Systems reasoning
definition: Explaining how interactions, feedback and delays produce the behaviour of a whole system over time.
medicine: A change that helps one part of a hospital can alter demand, flow or workload elsewhere. Seeing these connections helps doctors investigate persistent problems without attributing every outcome to individuals.
benefits: Trace how a delayed discharge affects several teams and the patients waiting behind it.
Identify feedback that amplifies or dampens a physiological change.
Explain why repeated local fixes fail to change overall service performance.
reasons: Feedback can sustain a problem after its original trigger disappears.
A delayed response can be mistaken for failure and prompt excessive correction.
A bottleneck can move after another constraint is relieved.
Improving a local metric can create costs outside its reporting boundary.
Drawing the boundary differently can reveal previously overlooked participants.
questions: Where would you draw the boundary of this problem, and who disappears when you draw it there?
Which consequence feeds back to change the condition that produced it?
What delay could make a helpful intervention look ineffective at first?
If one queue clears, where might the waiting reappear?
Which quantity accumulates over time and which merely describes the rate of change?
Two hospitals use the same protocol. Which difference in interactions might produce different results?
What behaviour would continue after the original trigger was removed?
Which locally sensible action could make the whole service less effective?
What early signal would reveal that feedback is amplifying a disturbance?
Which small change would distinguish a feedback explanation from a one-way chain?

name: Strategic reasoning
definition: Choosing a sequence of actions in light of future possibilities, dependencies and limited resources.
medicine: Clinical work often involves a series of decisions. The order affects what a team can learn, which options stay open and how readily a plan can be revised.
benefits: Sequence investigations so an early result can guide later choices.
Plan a staged service improvement around staff capacity and expected demand.
Preserve future options while making progress under uncertainty.
reasons: An early commitment can close options that later evidence would favour.
A useful first step may mainly create information for a later decision.
Resources spent early can constrain the response to a subsequent event.
A plan needs triggers for reassessment as conditions evolve.
Failure to anticipate dependencies can leave a sound next step impossible to execute.
questions: Which action today would most improve the options available at the next decision?
What must be in place before the rest of this plan can work?
Which early commitment would be hardest to reverse if your expectation proves wrong?
What evidence would justify waiting, and what opportunity might be lost while waiting?
How much of the plan survives if demand arrives sooner than expected?
Which resource is adequate now but likely to constrain the third step?
Where should you place a reassessment point so that new information can still change the outcome?
What would a reasonable backup plan need that the first plan also consumes?
If a short-term improvement undermines a longer-term goal, how do you compare the two?
How would your first move change if the expected follow-up could not occur?

name: Game-theoretic reasoning
definition: Reasoning about interdependent choices when each participant's preferred action depends on what the others are expected to do.
medicine: In healthcare, separately sensible choices by departments or organisations can produce an outcome none would choose together. Examining incentives can reveal ways to cooperate.
benefits: Explain why two services might each retain spare capacity despite a shared shortage.
Identify what information teams need before they can coordinate a handover.
Design a cooperative routine that remains attractive when demand increases.
reasons: A person's best response can change when another participant changes course.
Collective shortfalls can arise without ill intent.
Repeated interactions may support arrangements that would fail in a one-off encounter.
Uncertain information can make an apparently unhelpful choice understandable.
A credible commitment can change expectations before any resource moves.
questions: Which participants can act independently, and which outcomes does each actually value?
How would one ward's preferred allocation change if it knew the other would share spare capacity?
Could both teams improve their position while each has a reason to hold back alone?
What does each participant know when choosing, and which uncertainty concerns the other's choice?
If these departments expect to work together next week, how might today's choices change?
What small commitment could make a mutually helpful arrangement credible?
Which incentive rewards a local decision whose combined effect frustrates everyone?
How would you tell a genuine conflict of goals from uncertainty about whether others will cooperate?
Could a change in the order of decisions unlock cooperation without increasing resources?
What outcome would you predict if each group acted on an inaccurate guess about the others' priorities?

name: Adversarial reasoning
definition: Anticipating how a capable opponent or critic could challenge a claim, adapt to a rule or counter a proposed strategy.
medicine: A respectful challenge can uncover an unsupported assumption before a team commits to a diagnosis or policy. The object of scrutiny is the argument, and the person proposing it remains a collaborator.
benefits: Build the strongest competing account of a difficult case at a clinical meeting.
Look for a counterexample to a proposed clinical rule.
Review whether a policy could appear successful on its chosen metric while missing its goal.
reasons: A favourite explanation often receives less scrutiny than its rivals.
A weak objection can create false confidence that a proposal has been tested.
A convincing counterexample can reveal the boundary of a rule.
A fair challenge needs the same evidential standard on both sides.
Rehearsing disagreement makes it easier to revise a conclusion openly.
questions: If you had to defend the strongest rival interpretation at tomorrow's meeting, which finding would you lead with?
What is the most credible objection a well-informed colleague could make to your conclusion?
Which assumption would a sceptic challenge first, and how could you check it fairly?
Can you construct a case that passes the proposed rule but fails its intended purpose?
What answer would make a critic withdraw their objection rather than move the goalposts?
How would you test whether you are demanding stronger evidence from the rival explanation?
If people changed their behaviour in response to a new audit rule, which weakness in the rule would become visible first?
Which conclusion still stands after granting the strongest reasonable objection?
How could a quality measure improve while the experience it is supposed to represent worsens?
How would you invite a junior colleague to present disconfirming evidence without turning disagreement into a contest?

name: Optimisation reasoning
definition: Selecting the best feasible option for a stated objective while accounting for constraints, trade-offs and uncertainty.
medicine: Clinical services need to make choices with finite staff, appointments and equipment. Formalising the objective exposes whose outcomes count and which constraints are essential.
benefits: Balance appointment allocation against waiting time and access across patient groups.
Compare feasible staffing plans against a clearly stated outcome.
Identify a solution that remains acceptable when demand changes.
reasons: An easily counted objective can neglect an outcome patients value.
Hard safety constraints should be recognised before comparing feasible solutions.
Several options may involve trade-offs with no universally best choice.
A solution that is optimal on average can perform poorly under variation.
Finding the binding constraint can identify where extra capacity would matter.
questions: What precisely is being maximised or minimised, and whose outcome does it describe?
What makes a proposed option infeasible even when its average performance looks good?
Can one feasible option improve access without worsening any other agreed objective?
Which assumption about demand is doing the most work in selecting this schedule?
What happens to the best plan when a safety or accessibility constraint is tightened?
Which patient group could experience the longest delay under the plan with the shortest mean wait?
If an extra appointment became available, where would it make the largest difference to the chosen objective?
How much performance would you trade for a plan that remains workable on unusually busy days?
Is the apparent best option simply the best among the few candidates you considered?
What observation after implementation would tell you that you optimised the wrong outcome?

name: Instrumental reasoning
definition: Selecting means that can actually achieve a specified end and making the links from action to outcome explicit.
medicine: A clinical activity is worthwhile when it advances a goal that matters to the patient. Tracing that connection can expose missing steps or an activity pursued largely through habit.
benefits: Check whether a proposed investigation could change a decision the patient faces.
Align a follow-up plan with the patient's functional goal.
Distinguish completion of a discharge task from successful continuity of care.
reasons: A process measure can improve while its intended outcome stays unchanged.
A technically effective activity can fail when a necessary intermediate step is missing.
Different means can reach the same goal with different burdens.
A patient's objective may differ from the service's usual target.
Checking the means–end link can reveal when further action adds little value.
questions: What outcome is this activity intended to make possible for this particular person?
If the task were completed perfectly, what would still need to happen before the patient benefited?
Which possible result of this investigation would change a decision already under consideration?
Are you pursuing an intermediate target after the original goal has changed?
