What less burdensome route would reach the same patient-defined end?
Why should the proposed action influence the outcome in this setting?
What evidence would show that the chosen proxy has become disconnected from the patient's goal?
Who needs to act on the information once it has been collected?
Which available action looks productive but leaves the key obstacle untouched?
What would count as enough progress to stop adding further steps?

name: Second-order reasoning
definition: Tracing how the immediate effect of a decision changes the conditions or behaviour that produce its later consequences.
medicine: A sensible first effect can trigger a less obvious second one. A doctor uses this perspective to anticipate downstream workload, behaviour and patient experience.
benefits: Trace how a new alert could change staff attention over time.
Anticipate follow-up demands created by a change in testing policy.
Consider how modifying eligibility rules affects the people who seek care.
reasons: Immediate benefits are usually easier to measure than delayed costs.
People adapt to new rules and can change the outcome of a policy.
A new demand may appear in a team absent from the original discussion.
Delayed consequences can reinforce or undermine the original goal.
Defining the later outcome in advance makes unintended effects easier to detect.
questions: Once the immediate change occurs, what does it make easier or harder for the next person?
If every team adopted this individually sensible rule, what new problem could emerge?
What behaviour might people reasonably change after the new target is announced?
A reminder increases completed checks this week. How might its repeated use change attention next month?
Which group receives the benefit first, and which group inherits the later work?
Could an initially positive result increase reliance on a fragile part of the service?
What second consequence might offset the improvement visible on the dashboard?
How could a new eligibility boundary alter the mix of people counted as waiting?
Which later effect would you measure now so that its appearance could be recognised?
At what point in the chain do your assumptions become too weak to support a firm prediction?

name: Risk-based reasoning
definition: Comparing possible harms by considering their likelihood, severity, exposure and the uncertainties affecting them.
medicine: A rare event may matter if its consequences are serious, while a common minor burden can dominate the experience of many patients. Risk judgments make these differences explicit.
benefits: Prioritise safety reviews across events of different frequency and consequence.
Describe how a safeguard changes the likelihood or severity of harm.
Communicate residual uncertainty after a risk-reduction measure.
reasons: A raw count hides how often people were exposed to the hazard.
Rare severe outcomes can disappear in average performance measures.
Introducing a safeguard can shift risk to another group.
The same numerical risk can have different practical implications for different patients.
Historical rates can understate risk when circumstances have changed.
questions: What harmful event is being considered, over what exposure and for whom?
Is the apparent rise in incidents due to more exposure, better reporting or a greater chance per exposure?
Which matters more here: a small frequent burden or a severe uncommon outcome, and according to whose priorities?
Where does uncertainty about severity differ from uncertainty about likelihood?
Which group bears risk that is diluted in the service-wide average?
How would a proposed safeguard change the chain leading to harm?
What harm remains possible even if every part of the safeguard works as designed?
Which fact would make an earlier risk estimate unreliable in today's setting?
What is the cost of delaying action while trying to estimate a rare event more precisely?
How would you present both the absolute frequency and the consequence to someone deciding whether the risk is acceptable?

name: Decision-theoretic reasoning
definition: Choosing among actions by relating uncertain outcomes to their probabilities and to the value the decision-maker assigns to them.
medicine: Clinical choices frequently involve outcomes that cannot all be maximised together. A transparent comparison shows how evidence and personal priorities each shape a decision.
benefits: Compare options when one offers a higher chance of benefit at a greater burden.
Identify when new information could realistically change the preferred action.
Explore how a patient's priorities could alter the choice even with identical evidence.
reasons: The best-supported explanation need not imply a single preferred action.
A likely modest outcome and an unlikely valuable one can reverse rankings as preferences change.
An average benefit can conceal substantial differences in burdens people accept.
A decision may be robust despite uncertainty if all plausible estimates favour the same option.
Information has limited practical value when it cannot change the action.
questions: What actions are genuinely available, including deferring the decision?
For each option, what outcomes are possible and who judges their importance?
How could two patients prefer different options while accepting exactly the same probabilities?
Which outcome would a simple average fail to capture about this patient's priorities?
At what likelihood of benefit would the preferred option switch?
Would the uncertainty interval cross that switching point?
What additional information could change the decision enough to justify its burden?
How would you handle a consequence the patient finds especially difficult to trade against other outcomes?
Can you identify an option that is worse than another on every outcome the patient values?
If a reasonable choice leads to a poor outcome, what would you examine to judge the quality of the original decision?

name: Algorithmic reasoning
definition: Designing an explicit sequence of repeatable steps, conditions and stopping rules that maps inputs to an output.
medicine: A clinical pathway or audit procedure must handle ambiguous inputs, repeated steps and exceptions consistently. Testing those details can reveal where human judgment is needed.
benefits: Write a reproducible rule for selecting records for a quality audit.
Trace how a clinical pathway handles missing or contradictory information.
Identify an exception that calls for escalation to a human reviewer.
reasons: A rule that works on typical examples can fail at its boundaries.
An unhandled missing value can silently route a case down the wrong branch.
Repeated steps need a way to stop or seek help.
Order matters when one test changes the inputs available to the next step.
Explicit exceptions help distinguish a protocol's limits from errors in applying it.
questions: What information must be available before the first step can run?
If two conditions are true at once, which branch is taken and why?
What should happen when a necessary value is missing rather than negative?
Can two people following your written steps reach different outputs from identical inputs?
What boundary example would reveal ambiguity in the word “above” or “within”?
Could the process return to an earlier step indefinitely, and what condition should stop it?
Which step can be reordered without changing the result, and which cannot?
What example would expose a valid case omitted by your eligibility rule?
How would you revise one branch without changing the behaviour on cases that already work?
Where does the information become too ambiguous for an automatic next step to be justified?

name: Reverse reasoning
definition: Working backwards from a desired or observed endpoint to identify prerequisites and possible paths leading to it.
medicine: A doctor can start from a patient's desired function or a completed clinical event and uncover the steps that would have to precede it. Multiple paths may converge on the same endpoint.
benefits: Plan a return to a valued activity by identifying necessary intermediate milestones.
Trace a missing result back through the steps needed for its delivery.
Identify which prerequisite blocks an otherwise feasible discharge plan.
reasons: Working forward from habit can miss the prerequisite most relevant to the patient's goal.
A single endpoint can conceal several distinct routes.
A necessary condition can be mistaken for one sufficient to reach the outcome.
Some steps cannot be reconstructed uniquely from the final record.
A backwards plan can reveal the last point where an alternative was available.
questions: If the patient has reached their stated goal, what must already be possible immediately beforehand?
Which of those prerequisites is essential and which merely appears in the usual pathway?
Could another sequence lead to the same endpoint without passing through your proposed step?
A result is absent from a record. Which earlier events could independently explain that endpoint?
Which intermediate milestone would show that a planned route remains feasible?
What would you check first if two proposed paths share the same final step?
What does the endpoint fail to tell you about the order of earlier events?
How would you turn your backwards chain into a workable forward plan?
Which prerequisite consumes time that is hidden when you count only the final activity?
At what point does reconstructing an observed path require new evidence rather than further logical inference?

name: Divergent reasoning
definition: Generating several meaningfully different interpretations, questions or solutions before deciding which to pursue.
medicine: An initial explanation or familiar service model can narrow the search too quickly. Deliberately varying the underlying assumptions can produce options worth comparing.
benefits: Generate competing explanations when familiar labels leave key findings unexplained.
Develop several ways to meet a patient's goal under practical constraints.
Invite perspectives that reveal unconsidered approaches to a service problem.
reasons: Lists of near-synonyms can create a false impression of breadth.
A familiar example can anchor the options considered afterwards.
Using different starting assumptions produces alternatives that can be tested against each other.
Patients may identify a feasible option absent from a clinician's usual repertoire.
Separating generation from appraisal can keep an unfamiliar but promising idea alive long enough to examine it.
questions: If your first explanation were unavailable, what genuinely different account could cover the same findings?
Which two candidates on your list are actually the same idea in different language?
What possibility emerges if you begin with the patient's description instead of the existing referral label?
How many different routes could achieve the goal while preserving the patient's stated constraint?
What would someone from another profession notice that your current framing leaves out?
Which implicit assumption do all your candidate solutions share, and what follows if you vary it?
What explanation would make a currently awkward observation expected?
Could the same problem be changed at the level of a person, a team or a process?
What is one unfamiliar option that could be explored cheaply enough to earn a fair hearing?
Which proposed alternatives make different predictions and therefore justify keeping both on the list?

name: Convergent reasoning
definition: Narrowing a set of possibilities by applying explicit criteria until a choice or short list is justified.
medicine: A clinical team often has several defensible plans and little time to decide which deserves attention first.
benefits: Reduce a long handover list to the issues that need a decision.
Rank candidate explanations by the findings they must account for.
Agree with a patient on which remaining option fits their priorities.
reasons: It exposes criteria that quietly favour a familiar option.
It keeps clinical urgency distinct from explanatory likelihood.
It helps a team recognise when further elimination costs more than it gains.
It preserves a viable alternative when evidence is close.
It makes a narrowed decision easier to reopen when a key fact changes.
questions: Which criterion would actually remove an option from today's list?
If you could retain only two explanations, which observations must both accommodate?
Why did the most familiar option survive the last cut?
Which apparently decisive finding is shared by every remaining candidate?
What would change if the patient's chief priority replaced convenience as the deciding criterion?
Which low-likelihood possibility warrants a separate safety check, and why?
Where could several minor concerns be drowning out one decisive objection?
If the leading options tied, which next observation would break the tie?
At what point would another round of discussion cease to improve this choice?
What finding tomorrow would justify reopening the option you set aside?

name: Synthetic reasoning
definition: Combining separate pieces of information into a coherent account whose parts jointly explain more than any piece alone.
medicine: A patient's symptoms, physiology and daily experience often sit in different records. Joining them can reveal a relationship that each record obscures.
benefits: Connect observations from different professions into one case account.
Link a physiological change to a specific loss of everyday function.
Identify the piece of a referral that would connect two otherwise separate findings.
reasons: It helps prevent fragmented explanations across specialties.
It reveals dependencies that vanish in a list of facts.
It exposes an attractive story's unsupported connecting step.
It allows a patient's experience to revise a physiological account.
It produces an account a new clinician can reconstruct and question.
questions: What can the nurse's observation and the patient's account explain together?
Which finding changes meaning once the timing of the others is known?
What single connection would turn these three facts into an explanation?
On what evidence does that connection depend?
Which piece still sits awkwardly outside the account you have built?
If two findings share a cause, what third observation would become intelligible?
Which apparent contradiction calls for two interacting processes?
What would be lost if you presented the findings as separate problems?
How would you describe the whole account to someone who knows only one part?
Which new observation would force you to rebuild the links between the pieces?

name: Dialectical reasoning
definition: Developing an account through sustained examination of opposing positions, their assumptions and any revision that their conflict warrants.
medicine: Disagreement about care can reveal a hidden conflict over evidence, goals or the conditions under which a proposal works.
benefits: Represent two opposing recommendations fairly at a case conference.
Identify an assumption that makes both teams' observations intelligible.
Negotiate a revised plan whose justification each participant can inspect.
reasons: It reduces the tendency to defeat a weaker version of a colleague's argument.
It helps distinguish a factual dispute from a disagreement about values.
It makes revisions traceable to reasons.
It points out when apparent consensus hides an unresolved conflict.
It can uncover a better question than either side originally asked.
questions: What is the strongest version of the view you currently reject?
Which observation does each position explain unusually well?
What shared assumption might be responsible for the dispute?
Would the disagreement survive if both sides used the same outcome and time horizon?
Which concern raised by the opposing team should alter your original position?
Where would a compromise simply combine the defects of both proposals?
What third account could explain why each side has seen convincing evidence?
What would persuade each side to revise its view?
Which conflict remains even if both participants agree on all the facts?
How would you record the reason your final position differs from your starting point?

name: First-principles reasoning
definition: Reconstructing an explanation or solution from basic constraints and well-supported premises, then checking how the result depends on them.
medicine: Basic relationships such as conservation of mass help a doctor question a calculation or explanation that otherwise looks authoritative.
benefits: Reconstruct a balance equation when its remembered form is doubtful.
Check whether a proposed mechanism respects physical constraints.
Explain a familiar rule's scope to a trainee.
reasons: It reveals hidden assumptions in rules of thumb.
It permits progress when a memorised formula is unavailable.
It makes a units error visible.
It identifies conditions that break a useful approximation.
It distinguishes what the premises require from what still needs measurement.
questions: What quantities can enter, leave or accumulate in the system you are describing?
Which basic relationship would remain true even if your preferred explanation failed?
Could you reconstruct the equation from its units and physical meaning?
Which step in that reconstruction relies on an empirical assumption?
Where have you silently assumed a constant volume or steady state?
What would the simplest possible case predict?
Would the explanation still work if one input fell to zero?
Which measurement supplies information the basic principles cannot provide?
Why does a familiar rule work under these particular conditions?
What departure from those conditions would make the rule give the wrong answer?

name: Lateral reasoning
definition: Reframing a problem or challenging a tacit constraint to discover an approach that the initial framing concealed.
medicine: An apparently difficult clinical or service problem can persist because everyone has accepted the same mistaken description of it.
benefits: Reframe repeated missed visits around transport or access.
Find a fresh way of eliciting a history when a standard question repeatedly fails.
Reconsider whether a ward delay begins at the stage where it becomes visible.
reasons: It widens options when standard approaches repeatedly fail.
It makes arbitrary constraints visible.
It uncovers practical causes hidden by labels such as disengagement.
It generates inexpensive, reversible ways to explore a new frame.
It teaches the doctor to test an imaginative idea before adopting it.
questions: What part of the problem statement quietly dictates the sort of answer you are seeking?
How would the question change if the delay began one step earlier?
Which constraint did anyone actually verify?
If extra staff were unavailable, what feature of the process would you inspect first?
How would a patient describe this problem without the clinic's terminology?
Could the event being counted be a consequence of the problem?
Which apparently irrelevant observation becomes important under a different framing?
Could reversing the order of two steps remove the obstacle?
What small comparison could distinguish your new framing from the original one?
What evidence would make you abandon the clever explanation?

name: Generative reasoning
definition: Constructing candidate models, explanations or designs that satisfy stated constraints and have consequences that can be examined.
medicine: When the existing explanation fits poorly, a doctor needs alternatives concrete enough to be tested or discussed.
benefits: Construct rival models for an unfamiliar pattern of observations.
Devise a feasible alternative way of collecting a missing observation.
Create a follow-up plan around a patient's actual constraints.
reasons: It expands the pool of genuinely different explanations.
It turns an intuition into a model with identifiable assumptions.
It exposes designs that collapse under real constraints.
It teaches the distinction between novelty and explanatory power.
It creates predictions that let a team compare new ideas.
questions: Which observation must any new account explain from the outset?
Can you construct two accounts that fit the present facts through different mechanisms?
How would you change one assumption to generate a third possibility?
What relationship must your proposed model preserve?
Which feature of the new idea exists solely to rescue it from an inconvenient fact?
What observation follows from your proposal that nobody used to build it?
Can you invent a counterexample that the first model admits and the second excludes?
Which simpler design would deliver the same information?
Which of your proposals could another clinician test without your interpretation?
What would make the new account worth keeping after a familiar explanation improves?

name: Decompositional reasoning
definition: Breaking a complex problem into parts with defined interfaces, so that each can be examined and their interactions restored.
medicine: A symptom or a delayed care pathway can have several distinct components, each requiring different information.
benefits: Separate gait difficulty into initiation, balance, strength and endurance questions.
Divide a referral delay into sending, receipt, triage and booking intervals.
Allocate components of an assessment while preserving responsibility for their links.
reasons: It reduces overload during a complex assessment.
It helps locate the stage at which information is lost.
It makes dependencies between tasks explicit.
It prevents the same issue being counted under several headings.
It reveals when a tidy subdivision hides an interaction that matters.
questions: What smaller questions must be answered to resolve the original one?
Where would you place a boundary so that the pieces can be examined independently?
Which finding belongs at the interface between two parts?
Does the proposed breakdown cover every route through the process?
Could two components both be normal when their coordination fails?
Which subproblem should be examined first because the others depend on it?
Would a timeline reveal a different breakdown than a list of professions involved?
Which detail can you safely postpone without losing the original question?
What must each team member hand over for the pieces to fit again?
After solving the parts, what whole-system check is still needed?

name: Emergent reasoning
definition: Explaining how interactions among components produce a pattern at the group or system level that is difficult to see from one component alone.
medicine: Ward congestion, communication failures and team behaviour can arise through interactions among individually sensible actions.
benefits: Trace how small timing shifts across departments create a queue.
Explain why individually appropriate referrals overload a shared service.
Identify system changes that alter collective behaviour.
reasons: It helps avoid attributing a system pattern to one person.
It draws attention to feedback between local decisions.
It makes thresholds and sudden transitions easier to investigate.
It anticipates effects that appear only at scale.
It improves selection of measures that capture the collective outcome.
questions: Could every team be acting sensibly while the whole pathway deteriorates?
What interaction becomes possible only when several units share one resource?
Why might an extra arrival create a long delay on one day and none on another?
Which feedback could amplify a small disruption?
What group pattern would disappear if the units stopped influencing one another?
How could you distinguish a shared external cause from interaction among the units?
Which average hides the clustering that drives this outcome?
What would happen if two departments shifted their work by the same hour?
Which local improvement might worsen conditions for the whole service?
What measurement would reveal the collective pattern before an individual case draws attention?

name: Interpersonal reasoning
definition: Interpreting how interactions, roles and communication between people shape what they understand and do together.
medicine: A care plan often depends on whether patients, carers and clinicians can exchange information and agree who will act.
benefits: Notice when a companion's answers displace the patient's account.
Clarify an ambiguous handover between colleagues.
Repair a consultation when the participants have understood its purpose differently.
reasons: It reveals relationship dynamics that affect the history.
It exposes mismatched expectations before follow-up fails.
It helps clinicians invite disagreement across differences in authority.
It improves the allocation of shared responsibilities.
It makes communication repair possible after trust is strained.
questions: Who has had the least opportunity to speak, and what could that change?
What does each person believe the other has already explained?
Which interaction immediately preceded the patient's withdrawal from the discussion?
How could the consultation invite the patient's own view while respecting their companion?
Which request might sound routine to a doctor but burdensome to a family member?
What is a junior colleague risking by raising their concern here?
Who believes someone else now owns the next step?
How could you check whether a polite agreement reflects a shared understanding?
What would each participant say went wrong in the last conversation?
What observable change would show that communication between the parties has improved?

name: Mentalistic reasoning
definition: Inferring what another person might know, believe, feel or intend, while keeping those inferences open to correction.
medicine: A patient's words and choices make better sense when the clinician checks the beliefs behind them and allows the patient to disagree.
benefits: Explore what a patient understood a result to mean.
Notice a likely mismatch between the clinician's explanation and a family's interpretation.
Anticipate a listener's mistaken inference before a handover ends.
reasons: It helps a doctor distinguish observable behaviour from an attributed intention.
It makes misunderstandings easier to detect.
It reduces the temptation to treat silence as consent.
It supports communication adapted to the listener's starting point.
It encourages direct verification when several interpretations fit.
questions: What information was available to the patient when they made that choice?
What might the word “positive” have meant to them when they heard the result?
Which belief would make their apparently puzzling decision understandable?
What different belief could explain the same behaviour?
Which part of your account is observation and which part attributes an intention?
What might the patient assume you already know?
How could you ask about that interpretation without putting words in their mouth?
If the patient had understood the explanation differently, what might they have done instead?
How might distress change what they took from a technically accurate explanation?
What response from them would make you abandon your account of their thinking?

name: Motivational reasoning
definition: Investigating the goals, incentives and competing demands that may explain behaviour, and testing that account with the person concerned.
medicine: A plan becomes more workable when the clinician understands what matters to the person and what a seemingly simple action would cost them.
benefits: Explore why a patient prefers one follow-up option.
Distinguish an access barrier from ambivalence about a goal.
Find an outcome meaningful enough to guide a shared plan.
reasons: It helps prevent assumptions about effort or character.
It distinguishes a person's goal from the means offered to achieve it.
It reveals competing priorities that emerge only outside the clinic.
It helps a doctor recognise incentives created by the service itself.
It gives the patient a clear opportunity to correct an attributed motive.
questions: What goal might the person's choice be serving successfully?
Could the same action reflect a transport problem, a different priority or uncertainty?
What evidence would help separate those explanations?
What does the person say makes the proposed plan worth doing?
Which cost becomes visible only when you consider work or caring responsibilities?
Would the preference survive if the practical barrier disappeared?
What incentive might the clinic's booking system create unintentionally?
Are the patient and clinician pursuing different ends through the same proposed action?
What question would let the patient reject your account without losing face?
Which change in behaviour would genuinely test your proposed explanation of the motive?

name: Moral reasoning
definition: Judging what one ought to do by identifying obligations, harms, fairness and the reasons owed to those affected.
medicine: Everyday clinical work includes choices about honesty, respect and responsibility, even when the medical facts are clear.
benefits: Recognise when a convenient course shifts an unfair burden onto a patient.
Articulate why an error calls for an honest response.
Identify whose interests were overlooked in a routine decision.
reasons: It sharpens recognition of ordinary moral issues that can pass as logistics.
It separates the doctor's private preference from a defensible obligation.
It makes foreseeable harms to quieter parties visible.
It builds consistency across patients with similar claims.
It helps a doctor give reasons that a person affected can question.
questions: Who would bear the cost of the easiest course of action?
Which obligation applies even if nobody else will learn what happened?
Would you defend the same decision if the patient were less familiar to you?
What feature of this case could justify treating it differently from the last one?
Which harm would be avoided by speaking up, and which might speaking cause?
What promise, explicit or implied, has someone relied on?
Which person has a legitimate claim that has not entered the discussion?
Would a well-intended choice still be unfair in its effects?
What reason could you give directly to the person most disadvantaged?
After acting, what responsibility for explanation or repair would remain?

name: Ethical reasoning
definition: Working through conflicts among values, duties, rights and consequences to justify a course of action under uncertainty.
medicine: Knowing the expected clinical outcome rarely settles how to weigh autonomy, privacy, benefit or fair access when these pull in different directions.
benefits: Clarify which values conflict in a contested care decision.
Discuss a privacy concern alongside a family's wish to help.
Document why one course was preferred despite its moral cost.
reasons: It prevents a contested value from being presented as a medical fact.
It makes the patient's priorities visible in deliberation.
It motivates a search for options that preserve more than one value.
It supports transparent review of difficult trade-offs.
It identifies points where consultation or clarification of professional obligations is warranted.
questions: Which two legitimate commitments pull hardest in opposite directions here?
What factual uncertainty is making the value conflict harder to see?
Whose account of an acceptable burden is being used?
What option could preserve some of both interests at stake?
Which consequence would each person regard as hardest to reverse?
What further information could change the facts while leaving the conflict intact?
Would the chosen justification hold for another patient with different social standing?
Which voices should be heard before claiming that the trade-off is acceptable?
What would justify seeking an ethics consultation about this case?
What unresolved cost should be acknowledged to the person who disagrees?

name: Pragmatic reasoning
definition: Judging what a proposal would actually require and accomplish in the circumstances in which people must carry it out.
medicine: A medically sensible plan can fail at the point of travel, communication, cost, scheduling or follow-up ownership.
benefits: Check whether a patient can reach the proposed appointment.
Redesign follow-up around available communication channels.
Identify who will see and act on an outstanding result.
reasons: It exposes small operational barriers before they become missed care.
It distinguishes an attractive intention from an executable plan.
It helps design contingencies around predictable disruptions.
It reduces avoidable burden on patients and carers.
It favours outcomes that can be checked in ordinary practice.
questions: What exactly would the patient have to do between leaving today and the next review?
Which apparently small step depends on money, transport or digital access?
What happens if the letter arrives after the booking window closes?
Who will know if the referral never reaches its destination?
Which part of the plan is easiest to agree to and hardest to carry out?
How could a change in timing preserve its purpose while reducing the burden?
What useful option is available with the resources actually present?
What would the first sign of implementation failure look like?
How could the team check progress without transferring all the work to the patient?
What is the simplest contingency if the preferred route falls through?

name: Contextual reasoning
definition: Interpreting a finding or action in light of the setting, baseline, timing and circumstances that give it meaning.
medicine: The significance of a measurement, behaviour or research result can change when its conditions of origin change.
benefits: Interpret a change against the patient's own baseline.
Ask whether a study's population resembles the patient in front of you.
Distinguish a ward observation from the person's usual function at home.
reasons: It protects against applying a reference value without examining its conditions.
It makes measurement circumstances part of interpretation.
It reveals when a familiar label has shifted meaning across settings.
It improves decisions about whether evidence can travel to a new population.
It encourages explanations of why apparently similar cases differ.
questions: Under what conditions was this observation made?
How does it compare with this person's usual state on a similar day?
Would the finding mean the same thing during activity and at rest?
What change in setting could explain the apparent deterioration?
Which features of the study population decide whether its conclusion applies here?
What was happening immediately before the sample was taken?
Which detail would change the meaning of an otherwise reassuring observation?
How might the clinic environment alter what the patient is able to demonstrate?
What background assumption did the referring team reasonably make in its setting?
If you moved the same case to a different setting, which inference would you revisit first?

name: Narrative reasoning
definition: Organising events, experiences and interpretations into a coherent account while preserving uncertainty about sequence and cause.
medicine: A patient's story can reveal priorities and turning points that disappear in a problem list, while gaps in a persuasive story still need checking.
benefits: Reconstruct the timeline of a changing symptom.
Understand which loss the patient identifies as the start of illness.
Communicate a case history that distinguishes recollection from corroborated events.
reasons: It helps a doctor listen for events selected for their personal significance.
It reveals where accounts use different starting points.
It protects against equating a compelling sequence with a causal chain.
It improves continuity when a story passes between teams.
It creates room for a patient to correct a polished but misleading summary.
questions: Where does the patient begin the story, and why there?
Which turning point matters most to them even if the chart scarcely mentions it?
Which event is securely dated and which is reconstructed from memory?
What stretch of time has been compressed into a single phrase?
What second storyline could fit the same documented events?
Does the order of events justify the causal link the account implies?
Which details would you lose by retelling this solely as a symptom list?
Where do two narrators differ in emphasis while agreeing on the facts?
What would you ask before filling a gap in the story yourself?
What does the patient change when you read your summary back to them?

name: Perspectival reasoning
definition: Examining a situation from distinct vantage points and tracking how access to information, goals and responsibilities change what is visible.
medicine: Patients, families and professionals can each see a genuine part of a case that is inaccessible to the others.
benefits: Compare accounts of function at home and in hospital.
Identify whose observations are missing from a planning discussion.
Explain why two participants evaluated the same encounter differently.
reasons: It reveals information that a single professional role cannot supply.
It reduces overconfidence produced by one's own vantage point.
It distinguishes disagreement about facts from differences in priorities.
It helps reconcile apparently inconsistent reports across settings.
It supports fairer decisions when power affects whose view carries weight.
questions: What can the patient observe over a week that the team cannot see in ten minutes?
Which part of the decision is visible to the ward team but hidden from the family?
What would the account look like from the night shift?
Where do two descriptions differ because the observers saw different settings?
Which perspective has been treated as neutral simply because it is familiar?
If you swapped roles, which cost would become easier to notice?
Whose account would most directly address the disputed claim?
Can both sides be right about different parts of the same process?
Which viewpoint is absent because the person was never asked?
How would you combine the accounts while keeping their sources clear?

name: Metacognitive reasoning
definition: Monitoring how one's own reasoning is proceeding and deliberately changing the strategy, confidence or checking process when warranted.
medicine: A clinician can know many mechanisms yet still persist with the wrong method for the question at hand.
benefits: Notice when a vivid recent case dominates a judgement.
Switch from rapid recognition to deliberate comparison when a detail clashes.
Track where personal confidence and accuracy diverge.
reasons: It helps detect premature closure during familiar presentations.
It encourages calibration against outcomes and independent checks.
It identifies when memory load is larger than the actual inferential demand.
It guides decisions to slow down or seek a second view.
It allows a clinician to practise the step that repeatedly goes wrong.
questions: How did you arrive at the leading answer before you began explaining it?
Which part of your confidence comes from familiarity with the story?
What are you currently trying to do, and does that strategy answer the question?
Which piece of evidence did you spend least time considering?
What error does your usual way of solving this kind of case tend to produce?
Would writing the alternatives down change what you compare?
At what moment should you switch from recognition to systematic checking?
What independent check would challenge your judgement most effectively?
If your conclusion is wrong, which step was most vulnerable?
What could you compare with the eventual outcome to calibrate your confidence?

name: Epistemic reasoning
definition: Examining what a claim is based on, what its evidence warrants and what remains unknowable from the information available.
medicine: Clinical decisions draw on measurements, testimony, records and research that vary in reliability, independence and relevance.
benefits: Separate a directly observed sign from a copied chart assertion.
Explain what a result can establish within its measurement limits.
State explicitly which clinical question remains open.
reasons: It prevents repeated documentation from masquerading as independent confirmation.
It improves precision about the source of uncertainty.
It helps identify questions that require different evidence.
It supports honest explanations of uncertainty to patients.
It helps teams maintain provisional conclusions without turning them into permanent facts.
questions: Who first observed the finding, and who repeated it?
What would you still know if every copied mention were removed?
What exactly does this instrument measure, and how does that support the claim?
Which part of the conclusion goes beyond the data?
Can the current evidence distinguish absence from a failure to observe?
What sort of evidence would answer the remaining question?
Does the source have access to the event it describes?
Which uncertainty could better measurement reduce, and which would persist?
How strong a claim could you defend to someone with access to the same record?
What would make “we cannot tell from these data” the most informative answer?

name: Reflective reasoning
definition: Re-examining a previous judgement in light of its context, consequences and later evidence to improve future practice.
medicine: A completed case offers a chance to see how a decision was reached, including sound decisions that had poor outcomes.
benefits: Reconstruct a difficult consultation before the outcome was known.
Use feedback to identify an overlooked question.
Turn a case review into a specific change to test next time.
reasons: It limits hindsight distortion by recovering what was knowable at the time.
It separates the quality of a process from the luck of its outcome.
It surfaces habits repeated across otherwise different cases.
It turns vague unease into a targeted improvement.
It preserves helpful actions that an adverse outcome could otherwise obscure.
questions: What did you actually know when you made the decision?
What alternatives seemed plausible then, before the outcome became familiar?
Which judgment looks different only because you now know how the case ended?
What part of a good decision deserves preserving despite a poor result?
Which earlier cue takes on significance in hindsight, and was it usable then?
Where did the patient's account differ from your memory of the encounter?
What recurring feature links this episode with another difficult consultation?
Which specific action would you change in an otherwise identical future case?
What would you observe to tell whether that change helped?
What would a colleague who was present add to your reconstruction?

name: Critical reasoning
definition: Examining the premises, evidence and structure of an argument to determine how much of its conclusion is justified.
medicine: Clinical claims can sound persuasive while relying on an ambiguous comparator, an unmeasured assumption or a shift in outcome.
benefits: Interrogate the inference in a research abstract.
Identify an unsupported step in a referral's conclusion.
Distinguish an outcome meaningful to the patient from a convenient proxy.
reasons: It strengthens resistance to impressive but irrelevant statistics.
It reveals missing comparison groups and hidden assumptions.
It helps clinicians challenge claims constructively across seniority.
It clarifies exactly which part of a conclusion survives scrutiny.
It makes reasoning transparent enough for colleagues to audit.
questions: What is the precise conclusion the speaker wants you to accept?
Which premise carries most of its weight?
Would the result look different against a more appropriate comparator?
Has an association become a causal claim somewhere in the argument?
Which outcome was measured, and how closely does it track what matters to patients?
What assumption would a sceptical but informed reader dispute first?
Does the argument switch the meaning of a key term halfway through?
Which excluded cases could change the conclusion if included?
How much of the claim survives if its weakest premise is withdrawn?
What stronger argument could be made from the same evidence without overstating it?

name: Falsification-based reasoning
definition: Seeking observations that a proposed explanation cannot readily accommodate and specifying in advance how such observations would change it.
medicine: A clinician can accumulate compatible findings while overlooking the one feature that challenges a favoured explanation.
benefits: Specify what the current account predicts should be present.
Choose a check on which competing models give different expectations.
Reassess an unexpected result while considering measurement error.
reasons: It makes a favoured explanation genuinely open to revision.
It improves selection of informative observations.
It reveals ad hoc exceptions introduced to protect a fragile account.
It distinguishes a failed prediction from an unreliable measurement.
It helps teams agree in advance on when to reconsider.
questions: What observation would be difficult to explain if your preferred account were correct?
Which prediction did you commit to before seeing the result?
Would the test have been informative if either outcome counted as support?
What alternative makes a different prediction under the same conditions?
Could measurement error explain the failed prediction, and how would you check?
Which auxiliary assumption links the hypothesis to the observation?
How many exceptions have you added since the original proposal?
What evidence would favour replacing the model over adding another exception?
What would count as a meaningful challenge to a probabilistic prediction?
At what point would you tell the team that the original explanation no longer earns its place?

name: Heuristic reasoning
definition: Using a shortcut that exploits a recurring pattern to reach an efficient judgement, while monitoring when its assumptions fail.
medicine: Time and information are often limited. A useful clinical shortcut needs both a reliable cue and a recognisable point at which to stop using it.
benefits: Use a familiar pattern to focus the first questions.
State when a rapid judgement needs a fuller review.
Explain the working shortcut to a trainee together with its exceptions.
reasons: It improves selection of shortcuts suited to the local setting.
It makes the cue driving a snap judgement identifiable.
It reveals environmental changes that invalidate a once-reliable cue.
It helps prevent a memorable case from outweighing the base rate.
It reserves deliberate analysis for situations in which the shortcut is most vulnerable.
questions: What cue is doing most of the work in your first impression?
Why has that cue been reliable in your usual setting?
In which patient group would you expect the shortcut to perform poorly?
Is this example common, or merely easy to bring to mind?
What warning sign would trigger a slower assessment?
What would happen if the base rate changed but the cue stayed familiar?
How much would it cost to check the shortcut against one independent observation?
What did the last exceptional case reveal about the rule's boundaries?
Can you explain when the shortcut helps without presenting it as a law?
Which quick rule would you retire if its false alarms began to dominate?

name: Non-monotonic reasoning
definition: Revising or withdrawing a previously warranted conclusion when new information defeats an assumption on which it depended.
medicine: Records and handovers accumulate information. A later correction can invalidate several earlier inferences even when those inferences were reasonable at the time.
benefits: Withdraw an interpretation after a specimen is reidentified.
Trace which parts of a plan relied on an outdated history.
Communicate a changed working conclusion across teams.
reasons: It prevents outdated assumptions surviving in copied notes.
It separates a justified change of mind from an arbitrary reversal.
It exposes downstream conclusions that require a second look.
It helps preserve still-valid parts of an earlier account.
It teaches precise communication about what changed and why.
questions: What earlier conclusion was reasonable only while a particular assumption held?
Which new fact defeats that assumption?
Does the new evidence undermine the source, the rule or the conclusion itself?
If the specimen label was corrected, which interpretations must be revisited?
Which earlier conclusions remain sound after the correction?
Would restoring one missing detail reinstate the former conclusion?
What new exception limits a general rule you used yesterday?
Which entry in the handover could perpetuate the old inference?
What should a colleague learn about why you changed your view?
How would you distinguish justified withdrawal from overreacting to a single noisy result?

name: Ontological reasoning
definition: Clarifying what sorts of things a model describes and which relationships or properties can meaningfully belong to each kind.
medicine: Clinical records can confuse a symptom with a diagnosis, a measured value with a patient state, or a risk category with an event.
benefits: Distinguish a test result from the condition it is intended to detect.
Clarify what exactly is counted in a clinical audit.
Resolve disputes where one team uses a term for a process and another for an outcome.
reasons: It exposes category errors before they enter a clinical model.
It makes definitions consistent across records and research datasets.
It limits double-counting of overlapping entities.
It prevents a label from being mistaken for an explanation.
It reveals which distinctions matter when a case is reclassified.
questions: What kind of thing does this label refer to in the current record?
Are you counting patients, episodes, measurements or diagnoses?
Could one patient contribute several instances to the category you are counting?
Is this term naming an observation, an underlying process or a prediction?
What must be true for two entries to describe the same event?
Can the relevant property belong to a population while remaining undefined for an individual?
When a threshold is crossed, what actually changes in the world and what changes only in the label?
Which categories overlap, and what mistake would treating them as exclusive create?
What distinctions disappear when a continuous measure becomes a binary flag?
Would a different definition change the clinical question or only the coding?

name: Analogical abstraction
definition: Comparing cases to extract a general relationship that survives changes in their surface details, then specifying its limits.
medicine: A general structure can help a doctor recognise a familiar dependency in a new organ system or clinical workflow and test whether the analogy holds.
benefits: Derive a common bottleneck principle from a clinic queue and a laboratory backlog.
Recognise a shared balance between inflows and outflows in unrelated settings.
Reject a superficially similar case that breaks an essential dependency.
reasons: It makes existing knowledge retrievable in unfamiliar clinical settings.
It separates the essential relationship from vivid details.
It yields predictions that can be checked in a third case.
It exposes false analogies before they guide action.
It supports teaching a principle in a form a trainee can reuse.
questions: Which roles correspond across the two cases when their objects have different names?
What relationship remains if all the surface details are stripped away?
Which feature seemed central in the first example but disappears in the second?
Can you express the shared pattern without using vocabulary from either case?
What would the extracted principle predict in a third, unfamiliar situation?
What superficially similar example breaks one indispensable link?
Which quantity would have to be measured in the new setting for the mapping to hold?
At what level does the resemblance become so broad that it predicts nothing?
What exception sets the useful boundary of the principle?
Could someone apply your abstraction to a fresh case and also identify a near-miss?

name: Integrative reasoning
definition: Coordinating several forms of inference so that the output of one appropriately constrains the next and the combined judgement addresses the whole problem.
medicine: A difficult case can require explanation, prediction and a patient-centred decision. Each step has different evidence and a different standard of success.
benefits: Link a differential diagnosis to a test whose possible results would change the ranking.
Carry uncertainty from an inference into the discussion of options.
Combine physiological evidence with the patient's priorities without treating them as interchangeable.
reasons: It helps a doctor select the right operation at the right point.
It prevents uncertainty disappearing as information moves between stages.
It exposes conflicts between a plausible explanation and an appropriate action.
It makes multidisciplinary contributions mutually informative.
It enables review of which step limited the quality of the final decision.
questions: What question must be answered before choosing the next way to reason?
How does the explanation you generated determine which observations would now be informative?
What uncertainty in the first step should carry into your prediction?
Where might the most likely explanation and the most prudent next action diverge?
Which part of the case calls for a patient's value judgement and which for an empirical estimate?
What evidence would send you back to an earlier stage?
Which discipline could test a premise that your own approach takes for granted?
If two methods give different answers, are they answering the same question?
Where did confidence grow without any new evidence during the handover between steps?
How could another clinician retrace the whole judgement and pinpoint its weakest link?
